texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The house of Ninhursag at Kes is praised as the mother-temple of the land: the birthplace of kingship's blessings, its rites deep as the Abzu — the hymn copied as a school masterpiece for a thousand years.
summary.zh: 克什的寧鬍爾薩格神殿被頌為國土之母殿：王權祝福的誕生地，其祭儀深如阿卜祖——千年間為校中傳抄之名篇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The house of Kes, great house of Ninhursag, is praised: the mother-temple where the land's blessings are born, whose rites are deep as the Abzu and whose brickwork rises like the hills.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.2, the temple's praise; not verbatim.

passages.text: The hymn closes with the temple's charter: whoever honors the house of the mother goddess is blessed with kingship's favor — a school masterpiece copied for a millennium.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.2, the close; not verbatim.

functions: Classic of the temple-hymn genre
Charter of the mother goddess's sanctuary

variants.name: The temple hymns (corpus)
variants.summary: The full cycle of 42 temple hymns to which this belongs.

title.en: The Temple Hymns of All Sumer

region.en: From Eridu to Nippur and Lagash, Iraq
region.zh: 自埃利都至尼普魯與拉加什（伊拉克）

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript of an older cycle, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Forty-two temples from Eridu's Abzu shrine to Nippur's Ekur and Lagash's Eninnu are praised in order: a liturgical map of the land's sanctuaries, city by city, god by god.
summary.zh: 自埃利都阿卜祖神殿至尼普魯埃庫爾、拉加什埃寧努，四十二座神殿依序受頌：一座聖所的禮儀地圖，城以城計、神以神名。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn cycle; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The cycle praises forty-two temples in order: Eridu's house on the Abzu, Nippur's Ekur the navel of the land, Uruk's Eanna, Ur's house of Nanna, Girsu's Eninnu — city by city, god by god.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.1, the cycle; not verbatim.

passages.text: The map's order is theological: the temples are sung as stations of the world's order, each house holding its god's portion of the land's life — a liturgical geography of Sumer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.1, the geography; not verbatim.

functions: Liturgical map of Sumer's sanctuaries
Charter of each temple's cultic identity

variants.name: The Kes temple hymn
variants.summary: The most celebrated single member of the cycle.

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.4.80.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-310

title.en: The Ekur: House of the Mountain

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: A hymn to the Ekur (ETCSL c.4.80.4)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Enlil's temple is praised as the bond of heaven and earth: its foundations in the underworld, its crown in the sky, the place where the fates are decreed — the world's axis in brick and song.
summary.zh: 恩利爾之殿被頌為天地之紐帶：根基入冥界，頂冠接天穹，命運裁定之所——以磚石與頌歌築成的世界之軸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Ekur is praised as the bond of heaven and earth: its foundations reach the underworld, its crown touches the sky, and within it the fates of the land are decreed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.4, the praise; not verbatim.

passages.text: The hymn names the temple the place of Enlil's speech: what he says in the Ekur stands — the world's axis sung in brick and ritual.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.4.80.4, the decree; not verbatim.

functions: Theology of the Ekur as world axis
Liturgical praise of the fates-decreeing house

variants.name: A hymn to Enlil (Enlil A)
variants.summary: The god's hymn matching the temple's.

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript of an older text, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The antediluvian sage Shuruppak teaches his son Ziudsura the maxims of life — do not buy a wild ass, do not locate a field on the road, do not curse — the oldest instruction text, father to the wisdom books of the whole Near East.
summary.zh: 洪水前的賢者舒魯帕克訓其子祖蘇德拉處世箴言——勿購野驢、勿於路旁置田、勿咒罵——最古老的訓言文獻，近東智慧書之祖。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wisdom literature; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Shuruppak, son of Ubar-Tutu, speaks to his son Ziudsura: the instructions of the father to the son — a name to be given, a mouth to be held, a heart not to be trusted to strangers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.1, the frame; not verbatim.

passages.text: The maxims follow: do not locate a field on the road; do not buy a wild ass; do not swear; do not revile; do not lie in the assembly — the practical wisdom of the antediluvian sage that schools copied for two millennia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.1, the maxims; not verbatim.

functions: Oldest wisdom instruction text
Ancestor of the Near Eastern instruction genre
School curriculum masterpiece

primary_sources.citation: ETCSL c.5.6.1, trans. ETCSL team (2003-2006), lines 1-280

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: The god of agriculture instructs a farmer through the year: plough at the right time, let the flood come, guard the seed, harvest before the storm — the complete agronomy of Sumer in the form of a god's advice.
summary.zh: 農耕之神訓誡農夫一年之事：適時犁地、候洪水至、守種防鳥、風暴前收割——以神諭形式寫成的蘇美農學全書。

sensitivity.note: Ancient instruction text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The agricultural god instructs the farmer through the year: plough when the land is ready, let the flood-water come, keep the seed from the birds, harvest before the storms of the year's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.3, the instruction; not verbatim.

passages.text: The text closes with blessing: the farmer who follows the instructions shall fill the temple's granaries — agronomy taught as divine advice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.3, the close; not verbatim.

functions: Agronomy in instruction form
School text linking farming and liturgy

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: The three ox-drivers from Adab (ETCSL c.5.6.5)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Three ox-drivers from Adab dispute over one ox — each claims it — and the case is argued with proverb and precedent until the beast is shared: an early literature of dispute settled by wit.
summary.zh: 阿達布三名趕牛人爭一頭牛，各執一詞；以諺語與先例相辯，最後分牛了事——以機智了結爭端的早期文學。

sensitivity.note: Ancient humor text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Three ox-drivers of Adab each claim the same ox; their dispute is argued in proverbs and precedents, each man proving his right with a saying of the fathers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.5, the dispute; not verbatim.

passages.text: The case is settled by division rather than victory — the ox shared — and the tale closes laughing at the wit that ends what strength could not: an early literature of dispute settled by cleverness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.6.5, the settlement; not verbatim.

functions: Humorous dispute tale of legal wit
School text of proverb argumentation

variants.name: The debate poems
variants.summary: The formalized cousin of the dispute genre.

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: An elegy on the death of Nannaya (ETCSL c.5.5.2)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Nannaya, young scribe of the tablet-house, is taken by the underworld's fate; the elegy mourns him at the funeral — the bier, the mourning women, the procession — and consoles with the memory of his learning and love.
summary.zh: 書屋少年書記南納雅被冥界奪去；輓歌於葬禮哀悼——靈床、哭喪婦、送葬行列——以其學問與情愛之憶為慰。

sensitivity.note: Ancient elegy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nannaya, the young scribe of the tablet-house, is taken by fate; the elegy mourns him at the funeral procession — the bier carried, the mourning women keening, the friends following.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.2, the mourning; not verbatim.

passages.text: The consolation is memory: his learning, his love, his brightness among the students — and the underworld addressed as the household that now receives him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.2, the consolation; not verbatim.

functions: Personal elegy of the scribal world
Liturgical model of funeral mourning

variants.name: An elegy on the death of Nawirtum
variants.summary: The companion elegy for a woman.

primary_sources.work: An elegy on the death of Nannaya

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)

source.work: An elegy on the death of Nawirtum (ETCSL c.5.5.3)

texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: Nawirtum, the beloved of the poem's speaker, is taken young; the elegy mourns her with the imagery of the barren house and the wedding song now silenced — love's grief in the voice of the tablet-house.
summary.zh: 詩人的心上人娜薇爾圖姆早逝；輓歌以空寂之宅與戛然而止的婚歌哀悼她——書屋之聲裡的愛之慟。

sensitivity.note: Ancient elegy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Nawirtum is taken young, and the elegy mourns her in the imagery of the silenced wedding song: the house barren, the bed unslept, the streets she graced now empty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.3, the mourning; not verbatim.

passages.text: The speaker's grief answers the underworld directly — why was she taken before her time? — and the consolation offered is the memory of love: she is not forgotten while the song is sung.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.5.3, the grief; not verbatim.

functions: Love-elegy of the scribal world
Liturgical model of mourning a beloved

variants.name: An elegy on the death of Nannaya

primary_sources.work: An elegy on the death of Nawirtum

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A votive text presenting a new axe to the dread god: the smith's work praised, the god's terror described, and the offering's purpose spelled — appeasement of the lord of plague through gift.
summary.zh: 向可畏之神獻新斧之還願文：讚頌工匠之作、描摹神之威怖、陳明獻禮之意——以禮物撫慰瘟疫之主。

sensitivity.note: Ancient votive text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: A new axe is presented to Nergal: the smith's work praised in its cutting edge and weight, the god's terror named — lord of the plague wind and the battle's heat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.7.3, the gift; not verbatim.

passages.text: The offering's purpose is spelled: appease the dread lord, turn his face from the city, keep the plague away — gift as negotiation with the god of misfortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.7.3, the purpose; not verbatim.

functions: Votive offering text of appeasement
Document of the plague god's cult logic

secondary_sources.work: Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia
secondary_sources.citation: Jeremy Black and Anthony Green, London, 1992, entry 'Nergal'

texts.period: Old Babylonian manuscript, c. 1700 BCE (ETCSL translation 2003)
texts.license: ETCSL translation (Oxford, 2003-2006); quoted in paraphrase with attribution

summary.en: A votive text presenting a dog to the healing goddess: the animal as guardian of the sick-room and image of the goddess's own protective hounds — healing offered through symbol.
summary.zh: 向療癒女神獻犬之還願文：犬為病室之衛、女神護犬之像——以象徵奉獻療癒。

sensitivity.note: Ancient votive text; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: A dog is presented to Nintinuga, the healing goddess whose hounds guard the sick-room; the votive text praises the animal as image of the goddess's own protective pack.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.7.2, the gift; not verbatim.

passages.text: The offering asks the goddess to guard her suppliant as her dogs guard the sick — healing mediated by symbol and pack.
passages.note: Paraphrase of ETCSL c.5.7.2, the petition; not verbatim.

functions: Votive text of the healing cult
Document of the goddess's hound iconography

secondary_sources.work: Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia
secondary_sources.citation: Jeremy Black and Anthony Green, London, 1992, entry 'Nintinuga'
